checks.source_quote: Abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. checks.source_quote: Humanoid robots hold the promise of operating in environments designed for people, but doing so requires whole-body controllers that span diverse human motion, from locomotion and dance to crouching and balance recovery. Physics-based motion imitation addresses this by training RL policies to track reference motion clips [2] drawn from large motion-capture (mocap) datasets [1]. Existing systems scale this idea either by distilling many clip-specific experts into one controller [3] or by training a generalist policy over a large motion library [1]. In both cases, a more diverse motion library produces a more capable controller. But both also become computationally expensive as motion coverage grows: the state-of-the-art tracker SONIC [1], for example, trains for ∼168 h on 128 GPUs, totaling roughly 21,000 GPU-hours. Although reference motions differ, they share the same humanoid hybrid rigid-body dynamics. Model-free RL fails to explicitly model this shared structure, instead repeatedly

checks.assessment: 逐项核对：单一可微世界模型由 logged simulator transitions 拟合、BPTT 在短 imagined rollouts 上给出解析策略梯度、一个动力学模型在整个 mocap 库上摊销学习、梯度来自学得模型而非对模拟器求导因而兼容非平滑接触与不可微实现——初稿表述与原文一一对应，因果与方法条件均未越界，故逐字保留，未作改动。
checks.source_quote: SuperMimic addresses this inefficiency with a single learned, differentiable world model fit from logged simulator transitions. Backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) through short imagined rollouts provides analytic policy gradients through the learned model, allowing one dynamics model to amortize learning across the entire mocap library. Because these gradients come from the learned model rather than from differentiating the simulator, SuperMimic remains compatible with rigid body simulators, including those with non-smooth contacts and non-differentiable implementations.

checks.source_quote: Large-scale physics-based motion tracking. Physics-based motion imitation learns controllers that reproduce reference motions under contact-rich rigid-body dynamics. DeepMimic [2] demonstrated expressive character skills through model-free reinforcement learning, and PHC [11] extended this paradigm to large motion sets with robust recovery. SONIC [1] further demonstrated that scaling motion data, policy capacity, and training compute produces generalist controllers that transfer to humanoid hardware. These results establish motion tracking as a practical route to broad wholebody behavior coverage. However, training these large-scale motion trackers requires extensive simulator rollouts and substantial computation. SuperMimic addresses this bottleneck by learning a differentiable dynamics model shared across all motions, so policy improvement can exploit analytic gradients rather than model-free rollout estimates.

checks.source_quote: Learned differentiable dynamics for motion control. SuperTrack [12] optimizes motion-control policies through a learned differentiable surrogate of the simulator. ControlVAE [6] jointly learns a dynamics model, latent skill representation, and generative controller, while MoConVQ [13] extends learned-model training to discrete motion representations over tens of hours of data. SuperDyno [14] scales differentiable neural dynamics to tens of thousands of motion clips. These methods establish the effectiveness of learned dynamics and analytic policy gradients for scalable simulated-character control. SuperMimic extends this direction to single-GPU training of a large-scale humanoid tracker and to its sim-to-real deployment: its world model conditions on simulator context, while the de ployed actor uses noisy proprioceptive observations and a goal input (§3.2). checks.source_quote: Model-based policy optimization and robot deployment. Dreamer [15] and DreamerV3 [16] learn latent dynamics for imagination-based actor–critic learning, while TD-MPC [17] combines short-horizon planning with terminal-value prediction. DayDreamer [18] demonstrates world-model learning directly on physical robots. SHAC [19] uses differentiable simulation for short-horizon actor–critic updates, motivating SuperMimic’s critic-bootstrapped objective. Analytic-gradient robot control can also combine a simplified differentiable surrogate with a high-fidelity forward simulator, as demonstrated for quadruped locomotion [20]. SuperMimic learns its surrogate from simulator transitions and backpropagates through short imagined rollouts, retaining compatibility with standard rigid-body simulators.

checks.source_quote: RWM [21] and RWM-U [22] demonstrate that policies trained in learned neural simulators can transfer to physical robots. Both optimize policies using PPO on imagined rollouts; RWM-U additionally uses uncertainty-penalized offline optimization. SuperMimic instead optimizes the policy by differentiating the return through its learned dynamics. RWM and RWM-U pretrain the world model on trajectories from other policies. In contrast, SuperMimic fits its world model during training on data its own policy collects.

checks.source_quote: Reusable motion representations and downstream control. Reusable controllers connect motion tracking to downstream goal interfaces (Table 1). NPMP [5] and PhysicsVAE [7] learn latent motor representations from expert behavior; PULSE [8] and LATENT [10] use learned motion representations for downstream reinforcement learning. MaskedMimic [9] supports partial-body and multimodal goals through motion inpainting, while BeyondMimic [3] uses guided diffusion for goal following. SONIC [1] jointly trains goal encoders with its tracker using tracking rewards and latentalignment losses. ControlVAE [6] optimizes downstream task policies through its learned model while freezing the skill controller. SuperMimic jointly trains goal-specific encoders and a shared decoder through the same dynamics model (Appendix B). Goal interfaces can optimize either a reference-tracking reward or their own task reward. Our preliminary study trains a velocity interface concurrently with the motion-tracking interface

checks.source_quote: SuperMimic trains one goal-conditioned whole-body controller across a multi-skill motion library and supports multiple goal interfaces. It captures the shared humanoid dynamics in a differentiable world model and improves the policy through short imagined rollouts. Training alternates between three phases in one loop (Figure 2). First, the current policy collects simulator transitions into a replay buffer. Second, we fit the differentiable world model to short replay windows. Third, the policy is improved by backpropagating an imagined return through the frozen world model, with each rollout seeded from a replay-buffer state in the Dyna style [23, 24]. The buffer, model, and policy are updated throughout training, so dynamics learning and control improve together rather than in separate stages (Algorithm A.1, Appendix D). Transitions from earlier policies remain valid for fitting the world model, because the dynamics do not depend on the policy that collected them.

Each motion plays once from its first frame, with the same simulation for every policy: foot friction 1.0, no domain randomization or observation noise, and deterministic physics. checks.source_quote: Protocol. From standing, the policy receives a fixed command for 5 s; each command is tested in four trials. The relative steady-state error is the norm of the mean velocity error over the last 2 s, divided by the norm of the command, with the root velocity measured in the heading frame. The per-command value is the median over the trials that did not fall. The 672 step responses form a 15 × 15 grid on each of three planes, spanning the uniform command range above, with the standing command left out. In Figure 7, errors above 0.9 are drawn at 0.9, and a policy that fell in all four trials is drawn at the cap.

checks.assessment: 原文明确：单 GPU 3 h 内超过 SONIC 发布检查点的归一化回报、GPU-hours 减少超过 1000×（§4.1），129,514 动作基准上 3 h 单卡失败 25 个、9.8 h 双卡为 0（Appendix F）。数字与硬件条件（单卡 H100）一致；§4.1 另给出换算约 7200×，README 采用原文保守表述 >1000×，无需改动。
checks.source_quote: On one GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the normalized return of SONIC’s released checkpoint within 3 h and reduces GPU-hours by more than 1000× (§4.1). On a 129,514-motion benchmark, Super-Mimic fails on 25 motions after 3 h on one GPU and on none after 9.8 h on two GPUs, against 179 for SONIC’s released checkpoint (Appendix F). Across a 264× increase in dataset length, the world model’s prediction error stays stable and SuperMimic’s compute to a fixed return grows slowly. The learned policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1. In a preliminary study of downstream interfaces, an RL-trained velocity encoder outperforms a distillation baseline.

checks.source_quote: One model amortizes the motion library. In Figure 3(c), the world model’s 8-step prediction error stays between 0.007 and 0.011 as the dataset grows from 1 to 264 h. Every motion is executed by the same humanoid, so added clips supply more evidence about the shared body and contact dynamics rather than demanding new capacity. This is consistent with the slow growth of the compute needed to reach the target return (§4.1).

checks.source_quote: Figure 4(b, c) sweeps H with and without the critic. Without the critic, training fails at $H \leq 1 6$ With it, H=16 matches the critic-free H=32, and H=32 reaches a return of 0.82 fastest. Raising H from 64 to 128 nearly triples the time to that return and lowers the final return; H=128 is the longest horizon that fits on an H100. At matched return, the critic still changes behavior. Under 0.5–4 m/s velocity pushes while holding a static T-pose in simulation, the critic policy settles within 0.5–2.4 s. The critic-free policy never settles: it keeps stumbling even at 0.5 m/s and falls at 4 m/s.

The raw release contains 142,220 clips, but many interact with terrain or objects the robot cannot use (stairs, boxes, ladders, chairs) or carry retargeting artifacts that make them infeasible for a free-standing humanoid on flat ground. We remove these in two passes and keep 129,514 clips (Table A.7).

checks.source_quote: During each policy update, we hold the world-model weights $\omega$ fixed and optimize $\pi _ { \theta }$ and $V _ { \psi }$ on imagined rollouts of H=32 steps. This imagination horizon exceeds the k-step replay windows on which we fit the model (§3.2). In practice, the learned model remains stable over indefinitely long rollouts, because the k-step autoregressive fit trains it to correct its own prediction errors.

checks.source_quote: Compute accounting. The ratios compare SONIC’s reported 128 NVIDIA L40 GPUs for 7 days (about 21,000 GPU-hours) with 3 h on one NVIDIA H100, within which SuperMimic surpasses the return of SONIC’s released checkpoint. They are about 56× (> 50×) in wall-clock time and about 7200× (> 1000×) in GPU-hours. The 3 h cover the full training loop; checkpoint evaluations run after training and are not counted. SuperMimic trains on 264.56 h of motion from BONES-SEED [27], the public subset of SONIC’s data, about 2.3× less than SONIC’s 611 h. The GPU models also differ: in peak throughput, an H100 delivers 0.74× the fp32 and 5.5× the tensor-core performance of an L40; how much of that peak either run used is unknown. Nonetheless, 2.3× in data and at most 5.5× in peak GPU throughput cannot account for a 1000× gap in GPU-hours.
